GMIS 2026 · CTF write-up

How I Solved SENTINEL-07: From a Public Portal to Root

A first-person walkthrough of my GMIS Conference 2026 CTF investigation, with the reasoning behind each major decision.

The most useful file I found early in SENTINEL-07 was an onboarding memo. It gave me account names, confirmed that SSH was available, and turned a general search of a website into a specific plan for getting access.

That became the pattern throughout the solve: one finding made the next action worth trying. Public documents led to a weak-password login. A local permission mistake led to administrator access. Administrator access exposed the internal applications and their data.

SENTINEL-07 hosted the fictional OCI Citizen Report Portal in the GMIS Conference 2026 capture the flag competition. A CTF is a practice environment with deliberately planted security problems and hidden text values called flags. My engagement ended with 30 recorded flags, including the root objective.

This post explains what I did, why I did it, and what the results told me. The commands are excerpts from the investigation; the explanation does not depend on having access to the original machine.

Two exposed services gave me a starting point

I first checked my network interface and used Nmap to discover machines on the lab network. Nmap is a tool for finding hosts and identifying the services they expose.

ip a
sudo nmap -sn 172.30.30.0/24

My Kali workstation was 172.30.30.13. The target was 172.30.30.14, and the gateway was 172.30.30.1. Establishing those roles helped me keep discovery focused on the correct machine.

I then scanned the target’s TCP ports and examined the services I found:

nmap -p- --min-rate 10000 -T4 172.30.30.14
nmap -p 22,80 -sC -sV -O -oN nmap.txt 172.30.30.14

The useful results were Apache on port 80 and OpenSSH on port 22. A port is a numbered connection point for a network service. In practical terms, I had found a website and a remote-login service.

I started with the website because it was readable without an account. SSH was a possible next step if I could find credentials. Knowing that a login service existed was only the beginning; I still needed a way to authenticate.

The page source contained the first clues

I inspected the HTML rather than relying entirely on the visible page. Browsers receive comments, scripts, and hidden elements that may never appear on screen.

curl -s http://172.30.30.14/ | grep -iE 'flag|<!--|assets'

curl fetched the page. grep searched its text for likely clues, including HTML comments and references to supporting files. The pipe symbol passed the first tool’s output into the second.

The comment provided a flag; the JavaScript reference gave me somewhere else to look.

The comment contained {oci_serves_and_surveils}. A briefing hidden by page styling also included {lowercase_snake_case}, which was recorded as a valid flag.

The page referenced /assets/telemetry.js, so I inspected that file next. A build-tag comment held a Base64 value:

echo 'e2RlY29kZV9tZV9pZl95b3VfY2FufQ==' | base64 -d

It decoded to {decode_me_if_you_can}. Base64 is a way to represent data as printable text; it does not require a password or secret key to reverse it.

These findings collected flags, but they had not yet given me control of the machine. They did show that useful information was reaching unauthenticated visitors. That made a broader search of the public files worthwhile.

The onboarding memo made SSH worth investigating

I checked robots.txt and used Gobuster to request common file and directory names. robots.txt tells web crawlers which paths to avoid; it does not stop someone from visiting those paths. Gobuster helped find content that was not linked from the home page.

gobuster dir -u http://172.30.30.14/ \
  -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -x php,txt,bak

Among the useful discoveries were /backup/ and /dev/. The onboarding memo at /backup/onboarding_memo.txt exposed the logins riviera, armitage, and ashpool, as well as the retired accounts dixie and finn. It also confirmed that SSH was available.

The development changelog supplied another clue: fail2ban had been disabled. fail2ban can block sources after repeated failed login attempts. Its absence did not prove that any password was weak, but it made a common-password test against the disclosed accounts a plausible approach in this lab.

I built a short username list and used Hydra to test it against a password dictionary:

printf 'riviera\narmitage\nashpool\ndixie\nfinn\n' > users.txt
hydra -L users.txt -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \
  ssh://172.30.30.14 -t 4 -V

The recorded results included riviera:princess and armitage:blink182.

I connected as Riviera and obtained a terminal on the machine, whose hostname was case. This was my foothold: my first usable account on the target.

The connection between the findings mattered. A public memo supplied usernames, the scan identified the login service, and weak authentication turned that information into access. I could now inspect the machine locally, but I was still an ordinary user.

The name logscan hid a much more powerful program

Once inside, I looked for ways the account might gain additional permissions. This is privilege escalation. On Linux, the administrator account is called root.

sudo -l
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

The first command checked the account’s sudo permissions. The second searched for programs with the SUID permission bit. SUID can make a program run with its file owner’s effective identity, so a root-owned SUID program deserves close attention.

Two custom programs stood out:

  • /opt/oci/bin/evidence_archiver
  • /opt/oci/tools/logscan

I checked logscan --help to see what the program actually did. Its help text matched GNU env, a utility capable of starting another program.

That was the critical combination: a general-purpose command launcher with SUID root permissions. I used it to start Bash, a command shell:

/opt/oci/tools/logscan /bin/bash -p

Bash’s -p option preserved the privileged effective identity in this situation. The resulting shell could read files under /root.

The screenshot shows the escalation command and the protected files I could read afterward.

The final objective was in /root/final_flag:

{you_are_wintermute_now}

The submission value was CAHSI{you_are_wintermute_now}.

This was the decisive transition in the main solve. The weak SSH password had given me a user account; the unsafe SUID configuration turned that account into administrator-level access. The tool’s behavior and permissions told me much more than its logging-related name did.

Root exposed the applications behind the website

After reaching root, I searched the main evidence locations for the flag pattern and inspected the running Docker containers.

Docker runs applications in separate environments called containers. This host had three: the public portal, an internal case application, and a MariaDB database. The case application was bound to the host’s loopback interface, and the database had no published host port. They were not exposed like the public website.

But I now controlled the host and could use its Docker access to inspect those environments.

docker ps
docker exec ctf-portal-1 cat /var/www/html/config.php
docker exec ctf-casedb-app-1 cat /var/www/html/db.php

docker exec ran a command inside the named container. I read the configuration files because applications need connection details to reach their databases. Those files could explain how to connect without more guessing.

The portal configuration held {the_pay_is_terrible}. The case application used a different account: caseapp, with the password oci_internal_case_svc, connecting to the casedb database.

My initial database attempts had returned access-denied errors. Those failures showed why the account and connection method mattered. A credential from one component was not automatically valid in another.

The working session used the case application’s account over TCP. I also used PHP code inside the application container to reproduce its own database connection. Following the application’s settings gave me a connection that worked.

I listed the tables and read the two relevant ones:

SHOW TABLES;
SELECT * FROM users;
SELECT * FROM sealed_records;

A table organizes information into rows and columns. SELECT * asks for every column in the named table.

The database contained both an account-related flag and a flag inside a sealed case record.

Armitage’s stored case password was {corto_screaming_fist}. The sealed record OCI-0009 contained {sealed_records_never_sealed}. Dixie’s qwerty123 value also remained in the account table despite the account being marked decommissioned.

The challenge notes described a separate SQL injection route, where input could change a database query’s meaning. My demonstrated route here was direct database access after gaining root. Recovering the records did not establish that I had exploited the injection route.

The remaining files needed different kinds of inspection

Root access exposed more than database records. Backups, user notes, programs, and logs each held part of the remaining evidence.

The backup /var/backups/oci/shadow.bak retained old account material and a comment containing {decommissioned_but_not_deleted}. A Linux shadow file stores password hashes, which are used to check passwords. In this case, I could read the flag from the comment without cracking those hashes.

I used strings to extract readable text from the compiled oci-badge program, revealing {strings_never_lie}. A comment in the sudo policy files held {a_narrow_door_to_root}.

One file was more misleading: /root/incident_0472.pdf.

file /root/incident_0472.pdf
cat /root/incident_0472.pdf | gunzip

The file utility examines identifying bytes inside a file. It recognized gzip-compressed data, despite the .pdf extension. Decompression led to the recorded flag {magic_numbers_never_lie}.

The capture also includes an unexpected-end-of-file warning. That matters: recovering text from a compressed stream does not prove that the entire file is intact. The useful decision was to inspect the actual data format rather than trust the extension.

The logs produced another correction. My initial attempts used default Apache paths, but the useful log was /var/log/oci-portal/access.log. Searching it recovered {logs_remember_every_visit}. A failed lookup helped me refine where I was looking.

The archive password was a separate barrier

Ashpool’s three_jane_evidence.zip required another step. Root access let me obtain the archive, but the files inside still had password protection.

I prepared a copy named tj.zip, extracted its password-verification data with zip2john, and tested candidates with John the Ripper:

zip2john tj.zip > tj.hash
john tj.hash --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

zip2john did not decrypt the archive. It produced data that John could use to test candidate passwords. This was an offline attack against a local copy, unlike the earlier SSH attempts sent to the remote login service.

After recovering the password, I extracted sealed_evidence.txt and found {three_jane_holds_the_word}.

The extracted file confirmed that I could read the protected evidence.

The result depended on two failures working together: host compromise exposed the archive, and a password recoverable from a common list exposed its contents.

I separated recovered flags from demonstrated exploits

The target had other leads. The complaint form accepted PHP evidence attachments, and its template and challenge text pointed toward execution by a later processing service. My notes describe a reverse-shell route, where the target connects back and provides a command interface. The retained upload evidence shows acceptance of the file; it does not independently show that connection and its user identity. The associated flag was visible in a later search of the portal container.

The SUID evidence_archiver also referenced a helper resolved through PATH, the ordered list of folders searched for a program. That suggested a route in which a privileged program might run a substitute helper. The visible flag recovery, however, was a read of its proof file after the logscan escalation.

These distinctions are part of explaining the solve accurately. Collecting a flag after root is not proof that I independently completed every exploit suggested by its name. The clearest supported chain remains the SSH foothold, SUID escalation, and subsequent access to files and internal services.

What I took away from the solve

The investigation worked because each result answered a question and narrowed the next one.

The public documents told me which accounts to test. The SSH login let me inspect local permissions. The logscan help text revealed a dangerous capability behind an ordinary name. Root access exposed the application settings, and those settings explained how to reach the database. The remaining artifacts required attention to their contents and formats.

The defensive lessons followed the same chain: keep internal documents private, use strong authentication, limit privileged programs, and protect secrets and backups. Internal network placement also needs to be understood in context; it did not protect the database once its host was compromised.

I finished with administrator-level access and 30 recorded flags. What makes the solve useful to explain is the connection between those findings: how a piece of information became a reason to act, and how each action changed what I could investigate next.
